extracted.intended_audience: educated readers, students of literature/philosophy, and general readers of Montaigne
extracted.subtask_description: An early modern personal essay (Montaigne) offering moral and practical guidance about study, courage, nature, and conduct; the text mixes anecdote, classical quotations, and reflection. The page is a literary-philosophical essay rather than an explicit instructional rubric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Servare modum, finemque tenere, Naturamque sequi.
rubrics_metrics.description: “To keep a just mean, to observe a just limit, and to follow Nature.” (Lucan quoted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne presents this classical maxim as a guiding principle: avoid extremes and follow nature; value moderation over ostentation and excessive elevation in conduct and thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge and learning should serve the use of life
rubrics_metrics.description: The author praises those who 'proposed to himself no vain and idle fancies; his design was to furnish us with precepts and things that more really and fitly serve to the use of life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer practical, life-serving learning rather than learning for pomp or display; learning's merit is in usefulness to living, not mere ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer steadiness, simplicity, and ordinary pace to sudden elevation or show
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise for Cato: he 'ever creeps upon the ground, and with a gentle and ordinary pace, treats of the most useful matters' rather than 'mounted' displays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent, sober behavior and reasoned strength are preferable to striking but irregular brilliance; steadiness wins the understanding where agitation merely ravishes the judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware intemperance in the study of letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted: 'Ut omnium rerum, sic litterarum quoque, intemperantia laboramus.' (We carry intemperance into the study of literature, as well as into everything else.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive appetite for learning can be harmful; Tacitus' mother wisely restrained her son. Learning should be measured to avoid vanity, weakness, and mental overcharge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Little learning suffices to form a sound mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted: 'Paucis opus est literis ad mentem bonam.' (Little learning is needed to form a sound mind.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that beyond a modest amount, extra learning often brings feverish excess rather than real improvement of courage or moral fibre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Books often exercise the tongue more than fortify the will
rubrics_metrics.description: Books may enrich speech but do little or nothing to elevate courage; 'Books have not so much served me for instruction as exercise.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical that literary subtilties or eloquence replace the practical virtues required in real danger; some writings may only alarm fancy without strengthening character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between force and mere prettiness of style
rubrics_metrics.description: Warning: 'one ought to take a little heed not to call that force which is only a pretty knack of writing, and that solid which is only sharp, or that good which is only fine.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value substance and moral force over rhetorical cleverness; style should not be mistaken for moral or intellectual depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple, natural virtue surpasses obscure subtle science
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted: 'Simplex illa et aperta virtus in obscuram et solertem scientiam versa est.' (That overt and simple virtue is converted into an obscure and subtle science.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne praises rustic, plain virtue and cautions that learned systems can obscure and corrupt straightforward moral action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe ordinary people and even animals for moral exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne notes that unlearned people and beasts often exhibit constancy, patience, and natural prudence that sophisticated learning imitates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look to everyday life and nature for reliable moral instruction rather than assuming only learned authorities provide models of virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't over-anticipate or practise unnecessary forethought about evils
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of meditating on all possible disasters: 'What good will this curiosity do us, to anticipate all the inconveniences of human nature...?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipatory anxiety and rehearsing every calamity can burden the mind and cause more suffering than the events themselves; favour present enjoyment and proportionate preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation for death may cause more torment than death itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted: 'Minus afficit sensus fatigatio, quam cogitatio.' (Suffering itself less afflicts the senses than the apprehension of suffering.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical preoccupation with dying can increase anguish; natural courage often suffices at the moment of death without elaborate pretraining that troubles life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great courage speaks calmly; avoid passionate agitations as a sign of inner weakness
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted: 'Magnus animus remissius loquitur, et securius...' (A great courage speaks more calmly and more securely.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calm, measured expression of courage is a better indicator of strength than vehement or excessive displays of stoic exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline and strict enforcement sustain military order and public trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne contrasts French licence with the Turkish armies' strict penalties (e.g., severe punishment for petty theft) that preserve discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong, impartial discipline (even harshly applied for petty offences in war) prevents general licentiousness and preserves the common good; lack of discipline erodes public institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid violent reformation that destroys the commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato's and Favonius' position: one should not violate the peace of his country or 'cure' a government with civil war at the cost of citizens' blood and ruin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political remedies that hazard the lives and property of citizens are illegitimate; prefer prudence and prayer to destructive uprisings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware false religion that legitimizes wickedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted: 'Nihil in speciem fallacius, quam prava religio...' (Nothing has a more deceiving face than false religion, where divinity is obscured by crimes.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious or moral language used to cloak injustice is especially dangerous; scrutinize professed piety that sanctions wrongdoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate self-reliance and mastery of oneself
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted: 'Potentissimus est, qui se habet in potestate.' (He is most potent who is master of himself.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare to depend primarily on your own faculties and conscience in misfortune; true liberty is the ability to do what one wills with oneself.

rubrics_metrics.name: In widespread corruption, conserve conscience and prepare practically for necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne describes public disorder and argues one should ready oneself for change and rely on self-provided resources and discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When institutions fail, personal prudence and practical self-sufficiency (financial, moral) are necessary; cultivate habits to withstand civic disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy's preparation for death should not make dying dissimilar from living
rubrics_metrics.description: If one has not known how to live, 'tis injustice to teach us how to die, and make the end disform from all the rest; if we have known how to live firmly and quietly, we shall know how to die so too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral instruction should integrate with a life already well-lived; theoretical training for dying is pointless if it contradicts how one actually lives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mistake rhetorical subtlety for practical force
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne warns about 'slight and frivolous... verbal quirks' of writers that amuse but do not strengthen the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate ideas by their capacity to inform action and fortify character, not only by elegance of expression or novelty of argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value the natural acceptance and communal stoicism shown in crises
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts of plague: many people accepted death with little lament, renounced care of life, and displayed calm readiness; such ordinary fortitude is instructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is moral worth in communal, simple, unstudied resolution in face of mortal danger; such examples may be more authentic than contrived philosophical courage.
